regulatoryStatus: Not FDA-approved, and no marketing approval by any other regulator was identified; a preclinical research chemical (an NNMT inhibitor) with no registered human trials on ClinicalTrials.gov, sold as research-use-only material.

Not FDA-approved and not approved by any regulator identified. Its only registered human study was a first-in-human Phase 1 trial in metastatic prostate cancer, which was terminated at the investigator's request after enrolling four patients; no development has been registered since.

Not FDA-approved: its developer's Phase 2b obesity trial in 536 patients missed its primary endpoint and development was abandoned in 2007. FDA placed AOD-9604 in category 2 (significant safety risks) for compounding and in 2024 concluded the evidence weighs against adding it; the nomination was then withdrawn. WADA names AOD-9604 explicitly as a growth-hormone fragment (S2.2.3), prohibited at all times.

Not FDA-approved; cibinetide (ARA-290) is an investigational erythropoietin-derived peptide that has only reached small Phase 2 trials. FDA lists it in category 3 of the section 503A compounding nominations — nominated without adequate supporting information.

Not FDA-approved as a drug: acetyl hexapeptide-8 is used as a topical cosmetic ingredient, and US law requires no FDA approval for cosmetic ingredients other than color additives. It is listed in the EU cosmetic-ingredient database without any Annex restriction; no injectable or systemic use of it is authorized anywhere.
Not FDA-approved; sold for research use only; prohibited in sport by WADA

Not FDA-approved; an investigational long-acting amylin analog in Phase 3 development, studied largely in combination with semaglutide. FDA states plainly that cagrilintide cannot lawfully be used in compounding and has not been found safe and effective for any condition.

Not FDA-approved and holds no EU-wide marketing authorization from the EMA; a porcine brain-derived peptide preparation authorized nationally in individual countries (Austria has licensed it since 1996) and still trialed there for stroke.
Not FDA-approved; sold for research use only

Not FDA-approved. FDA placed dihexa acetate in category 2 (significant safety risks) for pharmacy compounding, stating it had identified no human exposure data for any route of administration; the nomination was later withdrawn, so it appears on no FDA bulks list.

Not FDA-approved. FDA placed emideltide — its formal name for DSIP — in category 2 (significant safety risks) for pharmacy compounding, citing an absence of safety information; the nomination was later withdrawn. FDA reviewed it again in July 2026 and concluded the evidence weighs against adding it to the compounding list.
Not FDA-approved; sold for research use only (a related pineal extract, Epithalamin, has been used in Russia; not approved in the US/EU)

Not FDA-approved and has no approved indication anywhere identified; the only completed trials of the FS344 sequence were early-phase gene-therapy studies in muscular dystrophy, not studies of an injectable peptide. WADA prohibits follistatin at all times as a myostatin-binding protein (S4.3).

Not FDA-approved as a drug; used as a topical cosmetic ingredient. FDA lists GHK-Cu for non-injectable routes in category 1 of the section 503A compounding nominations — under evaluation, not approved — while the injectable form was placed in category 2 for significant safety risks and its nomination withdrawn.

Not FDA-approved. Japan is the one country that has approved it: pralmorelin is marketed there by Kaken as a single-dose diagnostic for growth-hormone deficiency, not as a treatment. FDA placed injectable and nasal GHRP-2 in category 2 (significant safety risks) for outsourcing-facility compounding in September 2023 and lists it in category 3 under section 503A; WADA prohibits it at all times (S2.2.4).

Not FDA-approved. FDA placed GHRP-6 in category 2 (significant safety risks) for outsourcing-facility compounding in September 2023, citing effects on cortisol and insulin sensitivity, and lists it in category 3 under section 503A. WADA prohibits it at all times as a GH-releasing peptide (S2.2.4).

Not FDA-approved as a systemic or injectable drug; the only Drugs@FDA products containing a glutathione component are ophthalmic irrigating solutions. FDA lists it in category 1 of the section 503A compounding nominations — under evaluation, not approved — and has warned that compounded IV glutathione caused rapid adverse reactions traced to a supplement-grade ingredient.

Not FDA-approved for people today — Factrel (1982) and Lutrepulse (1989) are both listed as discontinued in Drugs@FDA, and the only current US approvals are veterinary products for cattle. In June 2026 FDA warned a seller that its 'Gonadorelin' is an unapproved new drug; WADA prohibits gonadorelin in males at all times (S2.2.1).
Not FDA-approved and no approval by any other regulator was identified; sold as research-use-only material. WADA prohibits hexarelin (examorelin) at all times as a GH-releasing peptide (S2.2.4).

Not FDA-approved and has no approved human indication; sold as research-use-only material. WADA names hGH 176-191 explicitly as a prohibited growth-hormone fragment (S2.2.3), banned in sport at all times.

Not FDA-approved and has no approved indication anywhere identified; a mitochondria-derived peptide that has never been given to anyone in a registered clinical trial — the studies naming it measure it as a biomarker rather than administer it.

Not FDA-approved; an engineered IGF-1 analog sold as research-use-only material. Recombinant human IGF-1 itself is approved as Increlex (mecasermin, 2005) for severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, but LR3 is a different, unapproved molecule. WADA prohibits IGF-1 and its analogs at all times (S2.3).
Not FDA-approved; sold for research use only (clinical development was discontinued)

Not FDA-approved — FDA states there is no approved product containing kisspeptin-10 in any country. FDA placed it in category 2 (significant safety risks) for section 503A compounding in September 2023, and its advisory committee voted 11-0 against adding it to the compounding list. WADA prohibits kisspeptin and its agonist analogs in males at all times (S2.2.1).
Not FDA-approved; sold for research use only
Not FDA-approved; an investigational oral peptide for celiac disease. Its Phase 3 trial (NCT03569007) was terminated by the sponsor in 2022, and no marketing application has been approved anywhere.

FDA-approved as Victoza (2010) for type 2 diabetes and Saxenda (2014) for chronic weight management, with generic liraglutide approved since; the EMA has authorized both. These are prescription injectables — research-grade liraglutide sold online is not an approved product.
Endogenous human cathelicidin peptide; synthetic LL-37 not FDA-approved; investigational only

Not FDA-approved as a drug: palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 is used as a topical cosmetic ingredient, and US law requires no FDA approval for cosmetic ingredients other than color additives. It is listed in the EU cosmetic-ingredient database without any Annex restriction; no injectable or systemic use of it is authorized anywhere.

Not FDA-approved. China's NMPA approved mazdutide in June 2025 for chronic weight management, adding a type 2 diabetes indication in September 2025; it holds no US or EU marketing authorization. FDA has warned a US seller that offering it online makes it an unapproved new drug.

Afamelanotide is FDA-approved as SCENESSE (October 2019) and EMA-authorized since December 2014 under exceptional circumstances, but only as a controlled-release implant placed under the skin by a healthcare professional, to reduce phototoxicity in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria. The injectable 'Melanotan I' sold online is not that product.
Not approved by FDA or EMA; an unlicensed drug sold illegally online as an injectable/nasal tanning and libido agent

Not FDA-approved; FDA lists mechano growth factor (MGF) in category 3 of the section 503A compounding nominations — nominated without adequate supporting information. WADA prohibits mechano growth factors at all times as growth factors (S2.3).

Not FDA-approved. FDA placed ibutamoren mesylate in category 2 (significant safety risks) for compounding, citing a trial stopped early over a congestive-heart-failure signal, and its advisory committee voted 13-1 against adding it to the compounding list in 2024. FDA also excludes ibutamoren from the dietary-supplement definition; WADA prohibits it at all times as a growth-hormone secretagogue (S2.2.4).
Not FDA-approved; sold for research use only (no approved human indication)
NAD+ precursors NR and NMN are sold as dietary supplements (NR/Niagen has US NDI/GRAS status); NAD+ itself and injectable/IV NAD+ are not FDA-approved drugs

FDA-approved only as an injection (Pitocin, 1980, plus generics) for initiating or reinforcing labor under direct medical supervision; the Syntocinon nasal spray is listed as discontinued in Drugs@FDA. Oxytocin sold online for other purposes falls outside any approved product.
Not FDA-approved and no approval by any other regulator was identified; an experimental neuro-active peptide with no registered human trials on ClinicalTrials.gov, sold as research-use-only material.

Not FDA-approved. FDA placed pegylated mechano growth factor in category 2 (significant safety risks) for compounding, stating it had identified no human exposure data for any route; the nomination was later withdrawn. WADA prohibits mechano growth factors at all times (S2.3).

Not FDA-approved: no FDA record of a drug or bulk substance under this name was identified, it appears on no FDA bulks list, and ClinicalTrials.gov lists no studies of it. It is sold as a variant of BPC-157 — a substance FDA evaluated separately in 2026 and proposed not to add to the section 503A compounding list, and which WADA names explicitly in class S0 (non-approved substances).

Not FDA-approved and no approval by any other regulator was identified; a synthetic tripeptide 'bioregulator' with no registered human trials on ClinicalTrials.gov, sold as research-use-only material.

Bremelanotide is FDA-approved as Vyleesi (NDA 210557, 2019) — a prescription autoinjector for acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women. 'PT-141' sold as research material is not that product.
Investigational; NOT FDA-approved (a triple GLP-1/GIP/glucagon receptor agonist in Phase 3 development)
Not FDA/EMA-approved; registered and used clinically in Russia as an anxiolytic (a synthetic analog of the peptide tuftsin)

FDA-approved as Ozempic and Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes (NDA 213051) and as Wegovy for chronic weight management (NDA 215256). Those are prescription products dispensed by a pharmacy. Research-grade semaglutide sold online is not any of them, and compounded or research semaglutide is the subject of a standing FDA warning.
Not FDA/EMA-approved; registered and used clinically in Russia as a nootropic/neuroprotective agent (a synthetic ACTH(4-10) analog)

Not FDA-approved today, though it once was: Geref was approved in 1990 and 1997, discontinued by its sponsor in 2008, and FDA formally withdrew both approvals effective June 2009 — not for safety or effectiveness reasons. Sermorelin now reaches buyers only through compounding and research channels; WADA prohibits it at all times as a GHRH analog (S2.2.4).
Not FDA-approved and no approval by any other regulator was identified; a preclinical ERR-agonist 'exercise mimetic' studied in rodents, with no registered human trials on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Not FDA-approved as a drug: acetyl octapeptide-3 is used as a topical cosmetic ingredient, and US law requires no FDA approval for cosmetic ingredients other than color additives. It is listed in the EU cosmetic-ingredient database without any Annex restriction; no injectable or systemic use of it is authorized anywhere.

FDA-approved as Forzinity (elamipretide, September 2025) under accelerated approval — the first treatment for Barth syndrome, in patients weighing at least 30 kg. That rare mitochondrial disease is the only authorized use; 'SS-31' sold as research material is not the approved product.
Not FDA-approved; an investigational dual glucagon/GLP-1 receptor agonist in Phase 3 trials for obesity and metabolic liver disease, with no marketing authorization identified anywhere.
Not FDA-approved; sold for research use only; WADA-prohibited (the full thymosin beta-4 protein is investigational as ophthalmic drug RGN-259)

Tesamorelin is FDA-approved as Egrifta (BLA 022505), and only to reduce excess abdominal fat in HIV-associated lipodystrophy — not for general weight loss or bodybuilding. Research-grade tesamorelin sold online is not that product.

Not FDA-approved and not approved by any regulator identified; an investigational triple monoamine-reuptake inhibitor whose developer has stated its Mexican marketing application was not approved. WADA prohibits tesofensine in competition as a stimulant (S6).

Not FDA-approved: in February 2024 FDA warned a US seller that its 'Thymalin' is an unapproved new drug and misbranded, rejecting the 'research use only' labeling. It is a thymus-extract preparation registered as a medicine in Russia but in neither the US nor the EU, and no clinical trials of it appear on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Not FDA-approved — FDA states it has approved no drug product containing thymosin alpha-1, and that Ta1 is not approved in the US, Japan, or Europe outside Italy. It is sold in some other countries as Zadaxin; FDA placed Ta1 in category 2 (significant safety risks) for compounding before the nomination was withdrawn.

Not FDA-approved. FDA placed the thymosin beta-4 fragment sold as TB-500 in category 2 (significant safety risks) for compounding, stating it had identified no human exposure data; the nomination was later withdrawn. WADA prohibits thymosin-beta-4 and its derivatives at all times (S2.3).

Not FDA-approved; FDA lists thymulin acetate in category 3 of the section 503A compounding nominations — nominated without adequate supporting information — and no registered clinical trials of it appear on ClinicalTrials.gov.

FDA-approved as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes (NDA 215866) and Zepbound for chronic weight management (NDA 217806), both prescription-only. Research-grade tirzepatide sold online is not that product, and the FDA has warned specifically about unapproved GLP-1 drugs sold for weight loss.

Not FDA-approved: two US emergency-use requests for aviptadil in COVID-19 respiratory failure were declined, and FDA lists vasoactive intestinal peptide in category 1 of the section 503A compounding nominations, meaning it is under evaluation rather than approved. A combination of aviptadil with phentolamine (Invicorp) is authorized in the UK for erectile dysfunction.
